transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um… yes. I suppose I’m here because occupational health asked me to come in. I don’t think I would have arranged it myself, honestly, because it’s sort of become part of my routine rather than something I was thinking of as a problem.

What’s been happening is that during lab runs, or when I’m helping with exhibition work, I tend to push breakfast and lunch aside. At first it feels practical, like I’m busy and I don’t want to interrupt what I’m doing, or I’ll tell myself I’ll eat once this stage is finished. But then the day gets away from me, and by the time I do eat, I keep it very small and controlled. It’s not usually a proper meal, I suppose. It’s more like something I can measure or account for, and then I feel… safer with that, in a way.

So, yes, occupational health picked up on it, or were concerned enough to send me here.
Do you find yourself avoiding eating because you're worried about gaining weight or because you're trying to control your shape or weight?

Yes… I think so. I don’t always phrase it to myself that way, because it sounds a bit stark when you say it out loud, but yes, weight is definitely part of it.

I do weigh myself, and if the number goes up even a fraction—honestly, even a very small amount—I get this sharp panic, like I’ve suddenly lost control, or like I’m becoming careless. It feels as if all the discipline I’ve worked so hard to maintain is slipping, and then I can’t really settle until I’ve done something to correct it. I know that probably sounds excessive, because logically I do understand bodies fluctuate, but in the moment it doesn’t feel like a normal fluctuation. It feels like evidence that I’ve failed somehow.
Have you ever made yourself sick or used laxatives, diet pills, or excessive exercise to control your weight or shape?

I’m… not really sure how to answer that neatly. I mean, I understand what you’re asking, but I don’t think I have a clear example to give you of that sort of thing.

I don’t think I’ve made myself sick, if you mean deliberately vomiting after eating. That’s not something I’ve noticed myself doing or planned as part of it. And with laxatives or diet pills, I can’t really say there’s anything like that I use in a deliberate way for weight control.

Exercise is a bit harder to define, because I do have days where I feel I should move more if I’ve eaten more than I meant to, but I don’t know whether I’d call it “excessive” in the way you mean. I suppose I wouldn’t want to overstate it. For me it’s more that I try to keep things controlled beforehand, if that makes sense, rather than doing something dramatic afterwards.
Do you feel that your weight or shape influences how you see yourself, to the point where even when others might not notice a change, you feel it very strongly?

Yes… yes, I think it does. Probably more than I like to admit.

It’s not even necessarily that someone else would see anything different. I can know, intellectually, that a colleague at the lab isn’t looking at me and thinking about my body at all. They’re thinking about samples, or timings, or whatever we’re meant to be doing. But when I’m getting ready in the morning, before I go in, I’ll look in the mirror and I don’t really see myself in a neutral way. I don’t look and think, “That’s just me.” I mostly notice my stomach, or my hips, and they seem… wrong, somehow. Too noticeable. As if they make me look careless, or unserious, which sounds strange when I say it out loud because obviously someone’s competence has nothing to do with that.

But it feels connected in my head. If I think my body looks bigger or less controlled, I feel as though that says something about me as a person, like I’m not disciplined enough or I’ve let standards slip. And then it can stay with me for the whole morning, even if nobody else has noticed anything at all. It’s very hard to shake once I’ve seen it that way.
When you look in the mirror, do you find yourself believing you are heavier or larger than you actually are, even when others might not see it that way?

Yes… I think that’s fair to say. It’s a bit difficult because in the moment it doesn’t feel like I’m “mis-seeing” myself, if that makes sense. It feels very real.

When I’m looking in the mirror before going to the lab, I don’t look at myself and think, “Oh, you’re thin,” or even just, “That’s my body.” My eyes go straight to my stomach or my hips, and they seem larger than they should be, or more obvious, like they’re the main thing about me. And then I get this feeling that I look careless, or sort of unserious, as if my body is giving something away about me not being controlled enough.

I know other people probably wouldn’t see it that way. I don’t think anyone at work is analysing my shape when I walk in. But I can’t seem to see it in that ordinary way myself. Once I’ve noticed those parts, they feel exaggerated, and it’s hard to believe they’re not as bad as they look to me.
Have these behaviors around food and body image started to affect your ability to function normally in your daily life, such as at work or in social situations?

Yes… I think it has, although I suppose I’m still functioning in the obvious ways. I’m still getting to work, still doing the lab work, still meeting the main deadlines. So if someone just looked at my output, they might not immediately think anything was wrong.

But it has changed things around the edges, and those edges are starting to matter. I’ve stopped going to lab lunches, for example. I used to go if people were getting something together or if there was a group lunch after a meeting, and now I almost always find a reason not to. I’ll say I’m too busy, or I need to check something, or I’ve brought work with me. It’s not that I don’t like my colleagues. I do. It’s just the food part makes it feel too exposed and difficult.

And there are informal planning meals for the gallery things as well, and I’ve pulled back from those too. I’ll suggest discussing things by email or say I can’t make it. Again, I can make it sound reasonable, but really I’m avoiding being in a situation where eating is part of the social thing.

So yes, I’m more isolated than I used to be. I don’t think I’ve completely fallen apart or anything like that, but my world has definitely got smaller.
Have you ever reached a point where your weight was significantly low, to the extent that you might be concerned about your health because of it?

Yes… I mean, I suppose that’s the uncomfortable part. I don’t always think of it as “significantly low” in the moment, because my mind sort of translates it into something else. But my clothes are definitely looser than they used to be, and the numbers on the scale have kept drifting down rather than just fluctuating normally.

There are moments where I can see that, objectively, I should probably be more concerned. Like when something that used to fit properly hangs differently, or I notice I’m checking the number and it’s lower again. A sensible part of me knows that isn’t just nothing.

But another part of me… and I know this probably sounds not quite right… sees it as evidence that I’m managing. That I’m focused. Especially when work feels chaotic or demanding, it feels like at least my body isn’t becoming another uncontrolled thing. It’s almost reassuring, in a way, which makes it harder to feel worried in the way I probably should.
Can you tell me approximately how much you currently weigh and how that compares to your weight before these behaviors started?

I… I’m a bit reluctant to give the exact number, if I’m honest. Not because I don’t know it — I do, probably too well — but saying it out loud makes it feel very concrete, and I find myself immediately wanting to justify it or explain why it isn’t as concerning as it sounds.

But compared with before all of this became so organised, I’m definitely down. It hasn’t just been normal up and down fluctuation. My clothes are looser in a way that’s hard to ignore — things that used to sit properly now hang differently, especially trousers and skirts. And the number on the scale has just kept drifting lower over time.

Part of me knows that’s probably the answer to your question, that yes, it’s lower than it was and not just by a trivial amount. But another part of me still reacts to it almost like it means I’m doing well, which is strange to say. Like I’m focused, or disciplined, or that I’m not letting the chaos and pressure at work spill over into my body. So even when I can see objectively that the weight is lower than before, emotionally it doesn’t register as danger straight away. It registers more like… control.
Can you tell me approximately how old you were when these behaviors around food and weight started, and how tall you are?

I’m not completely sure how to pin down the age, to be honest. I’m 40 now, but when you say “started,” I don’t know whether you mean when I first became a bit more careful about food, or when it became this more fixed, rule-bound thing. Those feel like slightly different points, and I don’t have a neat date in my head.

It wasn’t like one dramatic day where everything changed. It sort of crept in, and then at some point I realised it had become more organised than I’d admitted. So I can say it’s been a gradual process, but I’m not sure I could give you a reliable age without guessing.

My height… I should know exactly, but I’m hesitating because I don’t want to give you the wrong figure. I think of myself as around average height, but I don’t have the exact measurement in front of me. If it’s important, I could check or tell you what’s on my records rather than estimating badly.
